did_you_know.text: The title attributes the psalm to David and mentions Jeduthun: “For the director of music, according to Jeduthun.” The text itself does not explain Jeduthun’s exact role here.

The psalm begins with the word “Only,” emphasizing that the soul looks to God alone: “Only toward God my soul waits in silence.” The reason for this confidence follows immediately: “From him comes my salvation.”
God is described with three images of protection and stability: “my rock,” “my salvation,” and “my stronghold.” As a result, the speaker says, “I will not be greatly shaken.”

The enemies are portrayed as trying to bring someone down, using the image of an unstable structure: “a leaning wall” and “a tottering fence.” The picture emphasizes the danger of collapse and instability.
The psalm contrasts outward speech with inward intent: “With their mouths they bless, but in their hearts they curse.” It explicitly describes outward blessing alongside inward cursing and deceit.

In verses 6–7, the word “Only” appears again together with waiting for God. Verse 6 emphasizes hope: “For my hope comes from him,” while verse 7 repeats the images “my rock,” “my salvation,” and “my stronghold.”

The speaker expands personal trust into a call to all the people: “Trust in him at all times, you people.” He also invites them to share everything in their hearts with God: “Pour out your hearts before him.”

Human beings are described as “a breath” and “a lie,” and the verse adds that, taken together, they are light and have no real weight: “On the scales they rise; together they are lighter than a breath.”
The psalm warns against making three things the focus of one’s trust: oppression, robbery, and wealth. Even when “riches” increase, one must not set one’s heart on them.
The conclusion declares that power belongs to God: “Power belongs to God.” Immediately afterward, steadfast love is mentioned alongside it, so the closing message includes both strength and mercy.
